video.title: The Most Overlooked $1K/Hour Business Anyone Can Start

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Mike Herod about Voskills, a Florida trade school that runs woodworking and shop skills classes for children. Herod says the business began with a Facebook post and a few free classes, then grew through repeat students, homeschool groups, camps, school contracts, and state scholarship payments. The classes can be mobile and use simple projects and reusable tools; the transcript gives examples of pricing, costs, and revenue, though several figures are estimates or rough recollections. The core takeaway is to test demand with a simple offer, collect payment up front, keep projects safe and manageable, and use photos and word of mouth to build trust.

speakers.name: Mike Herod
speakers.description: Owner of Voskills, a trade school and shop class provider in West Palm Beach, Florida.

ideas.name: Children's woodworking and shop skills classes
ideas.one_liner: Run hands-on woodworking workshops, camps, and group classes for children, delivered at a shop or at the customer's venue.
ideas.business_model: Per-child hourly fees for small classes and events; camp fees; group contracts; some Florida families pay through the Step Up scholarship program.
ideas.customer: Parents of children, especially homeschool families and co-ops, private schools, and local groups. Herod describes age groups of 7–9 and 10+ and says the wider business serves ages 7–18.
ideas.problem: Parents have few places for children to learn practical shop skills, use tools safely, and build confidence through making things.
ideas.offer: Supervised woodworking and shop skills sessions using simple projects such as robots, flags, bird feeders, cornhole boards, and other kits. Formats include birthday and family events, recurring classes, foster community classes, school programs, and three- or five-day camps.

pricing.model: Per child per hour for many classes; fixed per-child camp fees; negotiated group contract pricing.
pricing.notes: Herod says he sometimes reduces per-head pricing for larger groups, but describes the 30,000 USD contract as having a different price structure. The transcript also mentions a 500 USD per-student skateboard class as a special project.

acquisition_channels.details: Started with a post on Herod's personal Facebook profile, then posted photos and updates consistently, reportedly every day.

quote.text: I just post. I just post pictures all the time.
quote.speaker: Mike Herod

acquisition_channels.details: Posted in homeschool and local mothers' groups; Herod says the business participates in three homeschool groups and describes them as tightly connected communities.

quote.text: And we're in three homeschool groups. One's got 9,000, one's got 5,000.
quote.speaker: Mike Herod

acquisition_channels.details: Free trial classes generated inquiries and referrals; Herod says homeschool families talk to one another and the business gained repeat students.

quote.text: It just becomes a word of mouth. It become word of mouth.
quote.speaker: Mike Herod

acquisition_channels.details: Created a Google profile and collected Google reviews; Herod says the profile was also needed for the trade school.

quote.text: We did a Facebook page and then then we did a Google profile
quote.speaker: Mike Herod

ideas.delivery: Herod, his wife, his son, and occasional helpers supervise children using hand tools and age-appropriate power tools. Classes take place at their commercial shop or at homes, parks, schools, and other venues. They bring tables, tools, and prepared project kits; sessions may be one-off events, recurring classes, or camps.
unit_economics_claims: Herod says a one-hour class for 10 younger children brings in 750 USD, with about 150 USD in costs and 600 USD profit.
Herod says the 30,000 USD, 14-week contract should leave about 10,000 USD after extra tools, materials, and staffing.
Herod says he made 50,600 USD from March through July, when classes were held at the commercial site.
Herod says spring break brought in 12,000 USD in one week, teaching only morning classes.
Herod says the hand-tool setup can cost about 425 USD and can be paid back by the first class.
ideas.startup_cost: Herod estimates about 425 USD for a basic hand-tool setup for six workstations. He says a very lean first class could cost less than 300 USD if the founder borrows a table and uses tools already available. A power-tool setup for six is estimated at about 4,100 USD.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. Herod says he posted around November 20, held two free classes, then booked paid events and classes in the weeks before Christmas.

acquisition.how: Posts and event listings can be scheduled, but the described acquisition depends on local community participation, photos, and human replies to parents. UK marketing rules also limit unsolicited electronic messages.

onboarding.how: A booking page and payment link can collect registrations and payment, but age suitability, venue details, consent, and safety questions need human review.

delivery.how: A qualified adult must supervise children using tools, teach the projects, and enforce safety rules throughout every session.

billing.how: Online checkout can take payment up front and reduce routine billing work; scholarship or group contracts still need reconciliation and human administration.

support.how: Parents ask about ages, dates, locations, and project suitability; an agent could draft replies, but staff need to handle safeguarding and individual needs.

uk_applicability.notes: The workshop format and parent-funded classes can transfer to the UK, with changes for safeguarding, insurance, venues, pricing, and local school or homeschool arrangements. Florida's Step Up scholarship vendor payments are specific to that state and do not transfer directly.

risks: A tool injury could seriously damage the business; Herod says to set firm safety rules and not relax them.
Children need close supervision, age-appropriate tools, eye protection, and projects sized to finish in the available time.
Parents may not consent to photos or videos being posted; Herod describes using waivers and excluding or obscuring children when requested.
The work is physical and locally delivered, so it cannot be run almost entirely by software agents.
A commercial venue may reassure parents but adds rent and operating costs; mobile delivery avoids some fixed overhead.
Florida scholarship funding and payment timing are not evidence of equivalent UK public funding.

tactics.name: Test the offer with a simple local post
steps: Describe one clear woodworking class on a personal Facebook profile.
Answer questions about ages, price, date, and venue as they come in.
Offer a small number of free sessions if needed to get initial photos, videos, and reviews.

quote.text: So yeah, Thanksgiving week I was like we need money and Facebook post woodworking birthday parties.
quote.speaker: Mike Herod

tactics.name: Collect payment before buying the first tools
steps: Set up a simple payment link with Square or Stripe.
Ask customers to pay in full or place a deposit before the class.
Use advance payments to fund the initial equipment and materials.

quote.text: They pay full out and use that three to five 700 dollars to frontload your first set of tools and then from there you're just repeating.
quote.speaker: Mike Herod

tactics.name: Use community groups and daily project photos
steps: Post in local homeschool groups and parents' groups.
Share project photos consistently so busy parents see the offer and the results.
Ask satisfied families to share the classes through their existing community.

quote.text: But it's all been Facebook. But, you know, listen to you and others posting consistently. Like, I have to post every single day.

tactics.name: Sell the outcome parents care about
steps: Lead with the confidence children gain from making something.
Describe the project and the benefit in plain language.
Use a simple image and invite parents to message for details.

quote.text: we don't teach woodworking. We help kids gain confidence through tools and woodworking.
quote.speaker: Mike Herod

tactics.name: Keep projects simple and repeatable
steps: Choose projects that use basic cuts, screws, and glue.
Prepare kits in advance and store them in labelled totes.
Reuse a small set of proven projects, while letting returning students choose a prior project.

quote.text: But really, I've got 10 projects, Chris, and that'll keep us busy for probably five years.
quote.speaker: Mike Herod

tactics.name: Set safety rules before every build
steps: Start each class with the shop rules and eye protection.
Set a firm boundary around tool use and do not waive it.
Match power tools to age and experience; younger children can use hand tools.

quote.text: Draw the line in the sand with safety and don't move an itch. Safety glasses.
quote.speaker: Mike Herod

tactics.name: Use large-group pricing when selling to an organiser
steps: Ask the organiser how long the session should run and how many students will attend.
Set a group minimum and maximum that match staffing and equipment capacity.
Price a contract separately from one-off per-child classes.

quote.text: And basically, I step down the the pricing, it's not, you know, $50 an hour. And basically tear it down basically, you know, like now our big ones is 30 kids minimum.
quote.speaker: Mike Herod

tactics.name: Create a separate vendor payment path for eligible families
steps: Register as an approved vendor in the applicable scholarship program.
Have the parent book the class and enter the code that zeroes out the checkout cart.
Direct the parent to submit the payment request through the program portal.

quote.text: They register on our line for the class, right, or book it and then they put a code in that zeros out the cart
quote.speaker: Mike Herod

tactics.name: Ask suppliers for sponsorship using customer lifetime value
steps: Contact a relevant tool supplier through a business contact on LinkedIn.
Explain how early tool exposure could build future customers for the supplier.
Use a customer lifetime value estimate in the pitch and ask directly for sponsorship.

quote.text: I just cold called a guy on LinkedIn. ... I put that in the pitch. I'm like I know these guys spend between 30 and $45,000 throughout their career.
quote.speaker: Mike Herod

tactics.name: Respect image consent
steps: Use a parent waiver that explains how photos may be used.
Mark which children may not be photographed or posted.
Exclude the child or obscure their face when a parent asks.

quote.text: So one thing I did learn is make sure to respect the um the parents that don't want their kids posted.
quote.speaker: Mike Herod

tactics.name: Offer a scrap-build option as an add-on
steps: Keep clean reusable offcuts from prior classes.
Offer a supervised free-build period using the scraps.
The host suggests testing an extra 10 USD per child for this option; this was a suggestion, not a reported sale.

warnings.warning: Safety is a non-negotiable: Herod says one injury could wreck the business. He requires eye protection and starts classes with safety rules.
Avoid projects that are too complex for the session. Herod says early classes ran long when he added paint and glue, then he simplified the projects.
Herod advises against using nails with children because he considers them an injury risk; he uses screws instead.
Parents may decline permission for photos. Use clear waivers and respect requests to leave a child out of posted images.
Herod says he initially overbought tools because he did not know what the classes needed; he recommends starting with a basic kit and borrowing where possible.
Herod says cheap lumber made the experience worse and later switched to higher-grade pine.
Florida's Step Up scholarship payments are location-specific; the episode's 24-hour payment claim should not be assumed to apply to UK funding.
The host and guest discuss the business in a promotional setting: the host solicits podcast applicants and paid community memberships, while Herod says Milwaukee supplied free tools.

evidence_quality.rationale: The guest is the operator and gives a concrete description of classes, equipment, pricing, acquisition, and delivery. Many figures are approximate, some are projections, and the transcript contains garbled captions and a few inconsistent statements about the share of girls in classes. The host also makes earnings projections that are not the guest's verified results.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: The host reads an Omnisend sponsor advertisement and promotes a paid channel community. The guest says Milwaukee supplied about 5,000 USD of tools; that in-kind supplier support may shape his favorable comments about its tools.
